title: Diversity in Animal Kingdom
tagline: The features animals are classified by, the great non-chordate phyla, and the five classes of chordates.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every phylum character, example organism and class feature below is standard animal taxonomy. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Animal classification exists because the animal kingdom is far too large to learn as a list, and the useful way to study it is to understand the characters that place an animal in one group rather than another. This chapter begins with those characters — symmetry, germ layers, the body cavity, segmentation and the notochord — and then works through the non-chordate phyla in the traditional order from Porifera to Echinodermata, giving each its defining feature, its body plan and a familiar example. The second half turns to chordates: the four characters every chordate shares, and the five classes of vertebrates, each treated by its distinguishing features, its method of respiration, thermoregulation and reproduction.

facts.label: Chordate characters
facts.value: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail

facts.label: Largest phylum
facts.value: Arthropoda, by number of described species

learningOutcomes: State the main characters used to classify animals and apply them to place an animal in a phylum.
Describe each non-chordate phylum from Porifera to Echinodermata with its defining feature and an example.
List the four characters of chordates and distinguish chordates from non-chordates.
Compare the five classes of vertebrates by covering, respiration, thermoregulation and reproduction.

learn.title: The characters used to classify animals

blocks.text: Before any animal can be placed in a phylum, five characters must be examined. The first is symmetry. Asymmetry means no plane can divide the body into equal halves, which is true of most sponges. Radial symmetry means the body can be divided into identical halves by any plane passing through the central axis, as in a hydra or a jellyfish, and it suits an animal that meets its environment equally from all directions. Bilateral symmetry means only one plane, the median plane, gives two matching halves, which produces a distinct head end and tail end and is associated with active directed movement. The second character is the number of germ layers: diploblastic animals have two, ectoderm and endoderm, while triploblastic animals have three, adding a middle mesoderm from which muscles, the blood and the excretory system develop. The third is the body cavity. In an acoelomate animal the mesoderm fills the space between the gut and the body wall completely, as in a flatworm; in a pseudocoelomate animal the cavity is only partly lined by mesoderm, as in a roundworm; in a coelomate animal the cavity is completely lined by mesoderm and holds the organs in fluid, as in an earthworm. The fourth is segmentation, the repetition of similar body units, and the fifth is the presence or absence of a notochord, which separates chordates from all other animals.

blocks.caption: Main characters used in animal classification
rows: Relates body plan to how the animal meets its environment
Number of primary tissue layers laid down in the embryo
Whether a fluid-filled cavity holds the organs
Repetition of body units allows regional specialisation
Present only in chordates; a rod of support for muscle attachment
All non-chordates, against a lancelet or a vertebrate embryo
Support and protection; limits or allows growth
Whether the first embryonic opening becomes the mouth
Worms and molluscs, against echinoderms and chordates

items: Radial symmetry suits a sedentary or floating life, since the animal meets the world equally on all sides.
Bilateral symmetry goes with cephalisation — the concentration of sense organs and nervous tissue at the head end.
Triploblastic animals have a mesoderm, which makes true organs and a body cavity possible.
A true coelom is completely lined with mesoderm, which allows the gut wall and the body wall to develop muscles independently.
Segmentation lets different regions of the body specialise, as in the head, segments and tail of a worm.
The notochord is a flexible rod lying just below the nerve cord, and in vertebrates it is largely replaced by the backbone.
An exoskeleton must be shed for an animal to grow, which is the reason arthropods moult.
Classification proceeds from the broadest character, the notochord, down to the class.

items.text: A flatworm such as planaria is bilateral and triploblastic but acoelomate: it has three germ layers, yet the mesoderm fills the whole space between gut and body wall so there is no cavity.
items.note: Germ layers and body cavity are independent characters and must be judged separately.

items.text: A grasshopper has an exoskeleton of chitin, so it must moult to grow; each moult leaves it soft and vulnerable for a period until the new cuticle hardens.
items.note: Exoskeleton and growth are linked, which is why moulting is a standard question.

learn.title: The non-chordate phyla from Porifera to Echinodermata

blocks.text: Porifera, the sponges, are the simplest animals: they have no true tissues or organs, and their bodies are perforated by numerous pores, ostia, through which water enters, flows past collar cells called choanocytes that capture food particles, and leaves by a large opening, the osculum. Their walls contain spicules of calcium carbonate or silica for support. Coelenterata, now often called Cnidaria, have a sac-like body with a single opening, the mouth, surrounded by tentacles bearing stinging cells called cnidoblasts used for catching prey; they are radially symmetrical and diploblastic, and they show an alternation of generations between a sessile polyp and a free-swimming medusa, as in Obelia, while Hydra is polyp only and the jellyfish is medusa only. Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, are flat, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate, with a sac-like gut and often a well-developed head with simple eyes; Planaria is free living while the tapeworm and liver fluke are parasitic and have lost the gut. Aschelminthes, the roundworms, are cylindrical, unsegmented, pseudocoelomate and covered by a tough cuticle, with Ascaris the familiar intestinal parasite. Annelida are the segmented worms: they have a true coelom, a body divided into repeated segments, and setae for locomotion, with the earthworm and the leech as examples.

blocks.caption: The major non-chordate phyla
rows: Porous body, choanocytes, spicules, no true tissues or organs
Cnidoblasts on tentacles, one opening, tissue-level organisation
Flat, leaf-like body, sac gut, often a distinct head
Cylindrical body, pseudocoelom, tough cuticle, unsegmented
True segmentation with setae, closed blood system
Jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, segmented body with head, thorax and abdomen
Soft body with a muscular foot, mantle often secreting a shell, radula
Spiny skin, water vascular system with tube feet, endoskeleton of calcareous plates
Radial as adult, bilateral as larva; coelomate

items: Porifera show cellular-level organisation only — no true tissue has differentiated, which is what sets sponges apart from all other animals.
Cnidoblasts are the stinging cells unique to Coelenterata, used both to paralyse prey and to anchor the animal.
The cnidarian body has two forms: the polyp, which is sessile and mouth downwards, and the medusa, which is free-swimming and mouth downwards beneath the bell.
Platyhelminthes are the simplest triploblastic animals, and their flat shape allows every cell to be reached by diffusion because there is no cavity.
Pseudocoelomate means the body cavity is only partly lined by mesoderm — it is not simply a smaller coelom.
Annelid segmentation is true metamerism: each segment has its own nerve ganglion, blood supply and setae.
Arthropoda is the largest phylum in the animal kingdom, and the presence of jointed legs is what the name literally means.
Molluscs use the radula, a rasping tongue-like structure, to scrape food; a bivalve such as a mussel has lost it.
Echinoderms possess a water vascular system that operates the tube feet used for locomotion and for gripping prey.
An adult starfish is radially symmetrical although its larva is bilateral, so symmetry must be judged on the stage being described.

items.text: A starfish feeding on a mussel uses its tube feet to pull the two shells apart steadily, then everts its stomach into the shell to digest the mussel outside its own body.
items.note: Shows the water vascular system in action rather than as a diagram label.

items.text: A tapeworm living in an intestine has no gut at all: its body wall absorbs pre-digested food directly from the host, and its flattened shape maximises that surface while its hooks and suckers prevent it being swept away.
items.note: Parasitic adaptation explains the absence of structures rather than merely noting it.

blocks.text: Chordates are distinguished by four characters that appear at some stage in the life of every member of the group, even though the adult may lose them. The notochord is a flexible rod of large vacuolated cells lying just beneath the dorsal surface; it provides a firm but elastic axis against which the longitudinal muscles can pull during swimming, and in vertebrates it is largely replaced during development by the vertebral column. The dorsal hollow nerve cord lies immediately above the notochord and develops into the brain and spinal cord; unlike the solid ventral nerve cord of a non-chordate, it is hollow, formed by the folding of a sheet of ectoderm. Pharyngeal gill slits are a series of openings in the wall of the pharynx, which in aquatic chordates become functional gills for gas exchange, while in terrestrial vertebrates they appear only in the embryo and are modified into parts of the ear and throat. The post-anal tail extends beyond the anus and contains muscle segments, helping with propulsion; it is retained in a fish but reduced in a human to the coccyx. All four characters are present in the embryo of every chordate, which is why the chordate larva, not the adult, is the reliable guide to classification.

items.meaning: Flexible rod of vacuolated cells providing an axis for muscle attachment; replaced by the vertebral column in vertebrates.
Nerve cord above the notochord, hollow in cross-section, giving rise to the brain and spinal cord.
Openings in the pharynx wall that form gills in aquatic forms and appear transiently in terrestrial chordates.
Tail extending past the anus, containing muscle and providing propulsion.
A chordate possessing a vertebral column that replaces the notochord.
Concentration of nervous tissue and sense organs at the head end, associated with bilateral symmetry.

blocks.caption: Chordate characters against the non-chordate plan
rows: Notochord present, later largely replaced by the backbone
No notochord; support by hydrostatic skeleton, shell or exoskeleton
Dorsal and hollow, above the gut
Ventral and solid, below the gut
Gill slits present at some stage
Tail absent or ends at the anus

items: All four chordate characters are most clearly seen in the embryo, and several are lost in the adult.
The nerve cord is dorsal and hollow in chordates, while non-chordates have a ventral solid nerve cord.
Gill slits are pharyngeal, not external openings, and they may be modified rather than lost in land animals.
The notochord gives support without rigidity, which is what allows the side-to-side swimming of a fish.
In humans the notochord persists only as small remnants within the discs between the vertebrae.
A lancelet shows all four characters in the adult and is therefore the classic non-vertebrate chordate.
The post-anal tail is the reason a human embryo briefly appears to have a tail before it is reabsorbed.
Having an endoskeleton allows continuous growth, unlike the periodic moulting required by an exoskeleton.

items.text: A human embryo at an early stage has a distinct post-anal tail, pharyngeal arches and a notochord, none of which is present in the newborn, yet all four chordate characters were demonstrably there.
items.note: Classification rests on embryonic characters as well as adult ones.

items.text: A lancelet buried in sand with only its mouth exposed shows a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, gill slits for filter feeding and a tail, so it is a chordate although it has no backbone.
items.note: Chordate is a wider category than vertebrate, and this is the standard example.

blocks.text: The five vertebrate classes are separated by covering, respiration, thermoregulation, the way the egg develops and the structure of the heart. Pisces, the fishes, are aquatic, cold blooded, covered in scales, breathe through gills supported by an operculum, and have a two-chambered heart pumping blood once through the body; their fins are for balance and propulsion and they lay eggs in water with little or no parental care. Amphibia lead a double life: adults have moist glandular skin without scales, breathe through the skin and lungs and, in many species, through gills that persist, are cold blooded, have a three-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle, and lay their shell-less eggs in water where the larva develops and undergoes metamorphosis — the frog is the standard example. Reptilia are the first fully terrestrial vertebrates: they have dry skin with scales or scutes, breathe only through well-developed lungs, are cold blooded, have a three-chambered heart in which the ventricle is incompletely divided, and lay amniotic eggs with a leathery shell on land. Aves are warm blooded, have feathers, forelimbs modified into wings, a four-chambered heart, pneumatic hollow bones that reduce weight, and lay hard-shelled eggs with extensive parental care. Mammalia are warm blooded with hair, sweat and mammary glands, a four-chambered heart, a diaphragm to assist breathing, and mostly give birth to live young that are fed on milk.

blocks.caption: The five classes of chordates compared
rows: Eggs laid in water, little parental care
Gills in larva, lungs and skin in adult
Shell-less eggs in water, larva metamorphoses
Dry skin with scales or scutes
Amniotic leathery-shelled egg laid on land
Mostly live young fed on milk

items: Amphibia are cold blooded and dependent on water for reproduction, which is why they are restricted to damp habitats.
The moist skin of a frog carries out respiration, so it must stay damp or gas exchange fails.
Reptiles evolved the amniotic egg, which freed them from returning to water to breed.
The incompletely divided ventricle of a reptile allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is tolerable for a cold blooded animal.
Birds have a four-chambered heart so that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood stay separate, supporting the high metabolic rate of flight.
Pneumatic bones contain air spaces and lighten the skeleton without sacrificing strength.
Mammary glands, which give the class its name, secrete milk and are found only in mammals.
A diaphragm is a muscular sheet that changes the volume of the thorax and so drives breathing in mammals.
Warm blooded animals maintain a constant body temperature, so they are active in cold conditions but must eat more.
Whales and dolphins are mammals despite living in water: they breathe air, have hair and nurse their young.

items.text: A frog breathes by three routes at once — the lungs when active, the moist skin continuously, and the buccal cavity by pumping air in and out — which is why a frog's skin must remain wet.
items.note: The three routes are frequently asked as a complete answer in themselves.

items.text: A crocodile has four chambers to its heart, unlike most reptiles, allowing a more complete separation of blood, yet it is still cold blooded and must bask to raise its body temperature.
items.note: Heart anatomy and thermoregulation are separate characters and need not match.

Beneath each, a caption line gives covering, respiration and heart chambers as two, three, three, four and four respectively.

keyPoints: Animals are classified by symmetry, germ layers, body cavity, segmentation and the presence or absence of a notochord.
Radial symmetry allows any plane through the axis to give equal halves; bilateral symmetry allows only one median plane.
Acoelomate animals have no body cavity, pseudocoelomate animals have a partly lined cavity, coelomate animals a completely lined one.
Porifera lack true tissues; Coelenterata have cnidoblasts and a sac-like gut with one opening.
Platyhelminthes are flat and acoelomate; Aschelminthes are round and pseudocoelomate; Annelida are segmented and coelomate.
Arthropoda is the largest phylum, characterised by jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton.
Mollusca have a soft body, a muscular foot and a mantle; Echinodermata have spiny skin and a water vascular system.
The four chordate characters are the notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail.
Pisces and Amphibia are cold blooded with two- and three-chambered hearts; Reptilia are cold blooded with three.
Aves and Mammalia are warm blooded with four-chambered hearts; mammals have hair and mammary glands.
examFocus: A phylum answer needs three parts — the defining feature, the body plan or cavity, and a named example — because any one alone is incomplete.
Do not say a flatworm is acoelomate because it is flat. Acoelomate refers to the absence of a fluid cavity between gut and body wall, which is a different observation.
The four chordate characters should be given as a set with the fate of each in the adult, since they are frequently asked as a five-mark list.
When comparing vertebrate classes, answer on the axes asked for — covering, respiration, heart, temperature and egg — rather than writing a general paragraph about each animal.

vocabulary.meaning: The arrangement of body parts about an axis, described as asymmetrical, radial or bilateral.
A body cavity completely lined by mesoderm in which the internal organs are suspended.
A body cavity only partly lined by mesoderm, as in roundworms.
Flexible supporting rod characteristic of chordates.
Stinging cell of cnidarians used to capture prey and for defence.
True segmentation, the repetition of similar body units along the trunk.
Network of fluid-filled canals in echinoderms operating the tube feet.
Maintaining a constant internal body temperature regardless of the surroundings.

questions.prompt: Which four characters are found in every chordate at some stage of its life?
options: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail
Exoskeleton, jointed legs, compound eyes, open circulation
Segmented body, setae, closed circulation, coelom
Water vascular system, tube feet, spiny skin, calcareous endoskeleton
questions.answer: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail
questions.explanation: These four are the defining characters of the phylum Chordata and each is present at some point in the life of every member, even if the adult loses it. The second option lists arthropod features, the third annelid features, and the fourth the features of echinoderms.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting all four in the adult. Several are embryonic only, which is exactly why the definition says at some stage of life.

questions.prompt: An animal whose mesoderm completely fills the space between the gut and the body wall, leaving no cavity, is described as __________, whereas one with a fluid-filled cavity completely lined by mesoderm is described as __________.
questions.explanation: Acoelomate literally means without a cavity, and the flatworms are the standard example because the solid mesoderm leaves no space. A coelomate animal has a true body cavity lined on all sides by mesoderm, which allows the gut and the body wall to develop their own muscles and move independently, as in the earthworm.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing acoelomate with pseudocoelomate. A pseudocoelom has a cavity, but only part of it is lined by mesoderm.

questions.prompt: Which feature is characteristic of phylum Arthropoda?
options: Water vascular system with tube feet
Jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton
Cnidoblasts on tentacles around a single opening
Body divided into segments each bearing setae
questions.answer: Jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton
questions.explanation: Arthropoda takes its name from the jointed appendages, and every member also has a segmented body protected by a chitinous exoskeleton that must be moulted for growth. The water vascular system belongs to echinoderms, cnidoblasts to coelenterates, and setae on each segment to annelid worms.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing segmented bodies as the distinguishing feature, since annelids are segmented too. It is the jointed legs plus exoskeleton that marks an arthropod.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which a sponge differs from a coelenterate such as a hydra.
questions.answer: A sponge has no true tissues or organs: its cells carry out functions individually and remain relatively unspecialised, whereas a hydra has true tissues, with muscle cells and nerve nets forming coordinated layers that let the animal contract and extend as one. Second, a sponge feeds using choanocytes, or collar cells, that create a water current and trap food particles inside the body, while a hydra captures prey directly with tentacles bearing stinging cnidoblasts and passes food into a sac-like gut through a single mouth.
questions.explanation: Two contrasts are asked for, and the two that carry most credit are the absence of true tissues in the sponge and the difference in feeding method. Each must be given on both sides, since a one-sided statement describes an animal rather than distinguishing two.
questions.commonMistake: Saying sponges have no mouth at all without adding how they feed. The sponge does have an internal cavity with an osculum, but food is filtered from the water current rather than taken in at an opening.

questions.prompt: Describe the body plan of an earthworm, referring to its segmentation, body cavity, symmetry and supporting features.
questions.answer: The earthworm is a bilaterally symmetrical animal, so only one median plane divides it into equal halves, and it has a distinct head end bearing sense organs. Its body is triploblastic and truly segmented: it is divided into a series of repeated units called segments, each of which has its own nerve ganglion, blood capillaries and small hair-like setae used in locomotion. Between the gut and the body wall is a true coelom, a fluid-filled cavity completely lined by mesoderm, in which the internal organs are suspended and through which the coelomic fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton against which the circular and longitudinal muscles can work. Support is therefore provided by the fluid in the coelom rather than by a skeleton of bone, and the worm moves by alternating contraction of circular muscles, which lengthen and thin the body, with contraction of longitudinal muscles, which shorten and thicken it.
questions.explanation: The answer must cover all four requested characters — symmetry, segmentation, cavity and support — and then explain how the muscles and coelomic fluid produce movement. Merely stating that the earthworm is segmented and coelomate without explaining the mechanism of locomotion loses the higher marks.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the setae as legs. They are small bristles that anchor segments against the soil, so movement depends on the muscles with the setae providing grip.

questions.prompt: Which class of vertebrates is correctly matched with its heart chambers and thermoregulation?
questions.explanation: Reptiles have a three-chambered heart, two atria and a single incompletely divided ventricle, and they are cold blooded, relying on external heat to raise their body temperature. Amphibians also have three chambers but are cold blooded, birds have four chambers and are warm blooded, and fish have two chambers and are cold blooded.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming birds are the only four-chambered group. Mammals share that arrangement, and no cold blooded class has four chambers apart from the crocodile among reptiles.

questions.prompt: An animal is found with the following features: it has a bilaterally symmetrical body, three germ layers, a body cavity only partly lined by mesoderm, an unsegmented cylindrical body covered by a tough cuticle, and it lives as an intestinal parasite. Identify the phylum it belongs to and give an example, and explain the significance of each of the first three features.
questions.answer: The animal belongs to phylum Aschelminthes, the roundworms, of which Ascaris is the familiar example. Bilateral symmetry means only one median plane divides the body into equal halves, which is associated with the presence of a definite head end and directed movement, and it shows that the animal is more organised than a radially symmetrical form. Having three germ layers means the animal is triploblastic: an ectoderm, endoderm and a middle mesoderm were laid down in development, and the mesoderm allows the formation of true muscles and organs. A body cavity only partly lined by mesoderm is a pseudocoelom, which is the defining cavity of this phylum — it is not a true coelom because the mesoderm does not surround the gut completely, so the gut wall and the body wall cannot develop entirely independent musculature.
questions.explanation: The identification rests on combining an unsegmented cylindrical body with a pseudocoelom and a cuticle, and the three features must then be explained individually. Bilateral symmetry speaks to the body plan, triploblastic development to tissue formation, and the pseudocoelom to the way the internal organs are held.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the cavity a true coelom because a space exists. A coelom must be completely lined by mesoderm, and a pseudocoelom by definition is not.

questions.prompt: Give two features that adapt a frog to its amphibian mode of life.
questions.answer: Its skin is moist, glandular and scaleless and is richly supplied with blood vessels, so it can carry out gaseous exchange directly and supplement the lungs; the skin must remain damp for this to work, which is why frogs stay near water. Second, the frog lays its shell-less eggs in water and the larva, a tadpole, hatches with gills and undergoes metamorphosis into the adult with lungs and limbs, so the aquatic larval stage allows development without the risk of the egg drying out.
questions.explanation: Both features must be tied to the double life of an amphibian: the skin links respiration to a dependence on damp conditions, and the mode of reproduction links the larva to water. Naming moist skin without explaining its respiratory role, or stating that frogs lay eggs without mentioning metamorphosis, earns only partial credit.
questions.commonMistake: Saying adult frogs have gills. Most lose them at metamorphosis; the adult breathes by lungs, skin and the buccal cavity.

questions.prompt: Which phylum is characterised by a water vascular system that operates tube feet?
questions.explanation: Echinoderms such as starfish and sea urchins have a water vascular system, a network of fluid-filled canals that opens to the outside through the madreporite and drives the tube feet used for locomotion, attachment and capturing prey. Arthropods have jointed legs, molluscs a muscular foot without tube feet, and annelids segmented bodies with setae.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing Mollusca because a snail has a foot. A molluscan foot is a single muscular organ, not the tube feet of a hydraulic system.

questions.prompt: The outer germ layer of a triploblastic animal is the __________, the inner layer lining the gut is the __________, and the layer between them, which gives rise to muscles and blood, is the mesoderm.
questions.explanation: The three germ layers are named for their position: ecto for outer, endo for inner and meso for middle. The ectoderm gives rise to the outer covering and the nervous system, the endoderm lines the alimentary canal and its derivatives, and the mesoderm forms muscles, the skeleton, blood and the reproductive system.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing ectoderm and endoderm. Remember that the nervous system, which develops from the ectoderm, lies at the outside of the body.

questions.prompt: Explain why a bird is classified as warm blooded and describe two structural adaptations that support its high metabolic rate, stating the function of each.
questions.answer: A bird is warm blooded because it maintains a constant internal body temperature irrespective of the surroundings, generating heat internally through a high rate of metabolism rather than relying on external sources of heat as a reptile does. This allows it to remain active in cold conditions and at night, at the cost of a much greater food requirement. Two adaptations that support the high metabolic rate are, first, a four-chambered heart in which the atria and ventricles are completely separated, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix and every tissue receives blood at the maximum possible oxygen concentration for sustained aerobic respiration. Second, the lungs are supplemented by air sacs that ensure a continuous one-way flow of fresh air through the lungs during both inhalation and exhalation, giving a far more efficient extraction of oxygen than the tidal breathing of a mammal. Hollow pneumatic bones reduce body weight, which supports flight rather than metabolism directly, but the heart and the air-sac system together supply the oxygen that the metabolism demands.
questions.explanation: The definition of warm blooded must be given as constant internal temperature maintained by metabolism, not merely as feeling warm. The two adaptations must each be linked to oxygen supply and aerobic respiration, since that is the basis of a high metabolic rate; describing hollow bones without connecting them to metabolism earns little.
questions.commonMistake: Citing feathers as an adaptation for metabolism. Feathers are insulation and are essential for flight, but they do not supply the oxygen the metabolism needs.
